result:
**Opening argument: C = 3√3/4**

The constant 3√3/4 is attained from both sides, so it is the best possible value.

**Lower bound (construction).** Take a bipartite graph with a base set B of about n vertices and reservoir vertices N = 1, ..., M, where reservoir vertex N is joined to g_N = (3√3/4)·d·n_B/√N base vertices. Every set consisting of the top a reservoir vertices and 2a base vertices has density exactly d, so d_{3/2}(G) = d. Solving the eigenvalue equations λK = (3√3/4)d·n_B·β and λβ ≈ (3√3/4)dK ln M gives λ² = (27/16)d²·n_B·ln M. Choosing M ≈ n/ln n yields λ = (3√3/4)d√(n ln n)(1+o(1)). So C cannot be smaller than 3√3/4.

**Upper bound (matching).** The sharp block lemma gives e(A,B) ≤ (3√3/2)·d·√|A|·|B| for |A| ≤ |B|. Its proof is direct: split B into blocks of size 2|A|, apply the density constraint to each set A ∪ B_i of size 3|A|, and optimize the block ratio, which gives c = 2 and constant 3^{3/2}/2. Writing λ = 2∬F(s,t) ds dt and applying this lemma to the dominant region s > t, the resulting functional is maximized at c = 1 with value √c/(1+c) = 1/2. This gives λ ≤ (3√3/4)d√(n ln n)(1+o(1)). The region s ≤ t contributes only O(λ/(ln n)²).

**Why the log appears at p = 3/2.** For the reservoir profile x(N) ∝ N^{-(2-p)}, the base equation involves Σ N^{2p-4}. This sum is logarithmic exactly when p = 3/2, which explains the √(log n) factor at the transition.

Both bounds coincide, so C = (3√3/2)·(1/2) = 3√3/4 ≈ 1.299.
